id: #104 from The Poems of Gaius Valerius Catullus

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

with Dana Ward with Dana Ward I have so little want of activity even writing with its pain more terrible than life I don’t want but do because I’m kind of stupid finally not in the way, you, Sarah know I am nor, you reader, who think of me fishing. Line, spindle, lure, bait. Instruments for me are accessories, even the matchbook is only a tiara to my eyes, the fishing lure a long & white bracelet. Some of my so-called friends think of me as a derelict they always try to hold me to account. “Tell me what happened on the drunken night in question” On the witness stand I am a kitten terribly cute but I can’t say a thing about stupid, or fish, or last night. I like to lay at the base of a hill asleep while the shepherds work bringing things to heel with tepid will where I source my contempt in the index of swill. The entries there make no mention of hell which was sifted through the vale of tears, & fell to make Earth, & the base of this hill where I sunbathe & murmur ‘jealous cellmate’ as my willful peers go by.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Dana, Ward, Sarah

outputs.L1:
With Dana Ward, with Dana Ward, I have so little want of activity—even writing, with its pain more terrible than life. I don’t want to, but I do, because I’m kind of stupid; finally, not in the way you, Sarah, know I am, nor in the way you, reader, who think of me fishing. Line, spindle, lure, bait. Instruments, for me, are accessories; even the matchbook is only a tiara to my eyes, the fishing lure a long, white bracelet.

Some of my so-called friends think of me as a derelict; they always try to hold me to account. “Tell me what happened on the drunken night in question.” On the witness stand, I am a kitten—terribly cute—but I can’t say a thing about stupid, or fish, or last night.

I like to lie at the base of a hill, asleep, while the shepherds work, bringing things to heel with tepid will, where I source my contempt in the index of swill. The entries there make no mention of hell, which was sifted through the vale of tears and fell to make Earth, and the base of this hill where I sunbathe and murmur “jealous cellmate” as my willful peers go by.
outputs.L2:
Together with Dana Ward—again, with Dana Ward—I feel almost no desire to do anything at all, not even to write, since writing hurts in a way more frightening than living. I do not want to, yet I do it anyway, because in the end I am somewhat foolish—not in the sense that you, Sarah, understand me to be, and not in the sense imagined by you, reader, when you picture me angling.  

Thread, reel, hook, bait: such tools are merely adornments to me. Even a matchbook appears to my eyes like a crown, and a fishing lure looks like a pale, elongated bangle. A few of the people who call themselves my friends regard me as some ruined stray, and they are forever trying to make me answer for myself. “Explain what occurred on the intoxicated evening under discussion,” they demand.  

Placed before judgment, I become a tiny, unbearably adorable cat, unable to utter anything about foolishness, or fish, or what took place the previous night. I prefer to sleep at the foot of a slope while the shepherds go about their labor, weakly forcing matters into order, and from there I draw my scorn from a catalog of refuse. Its listings say nothing of hell, which was strained through the valley of sorrow and dropped down to form the world, and also the bottom of this hill, where I lie in the sun and whisper “envious prison companion” while my stubborn equals pass by.
outputs.L3:
The speaker presents themselves as someone with very little desire for activity of any kind. Even writing, which might normally be seen as a purposeful or expressive act, feels painful to them. Yet despite this pain, they also seem compelled to continue doing it, as if writing is both a burden and an unavoidable necessity.

At the same time, the speaker resists the way others define or judge them. They reject the assumption that they are stupid, or that their identity can be reduced to any simple label. In particular, they push back against being associated with fishing, refusing to accept the idea that fishing describes who they are or what they care about.

This rejection extends to the objects around them. Everyday items and fishing tools are not valued for their practical use. Instead, the speaker sees them more as decorative accessories, objects that contribute to an appearance or atmosphere rather than serving any real function. This suggests a distance between the speaker and the ordinary purposes of the world around them.

The speaker also feels watched and judged by their friends. They believe their friends treat them as if they are responsible for some past drunken behavior, holding them accountable for actions or mistakes that continue to define how others see them. This creates a sense of resentment and discomfort, as though the speaker is trapped beneath other people’s expectations and memories.

Finally, the speaker imagines themselves in a passive position, resting while others work. This image reinforces their detachment from the people around them. Rather than feeling solidarity with their peers, they express contempt and alienation. They seem to see others as busy, conventional, or judgmental, while they remain apart from them, unwilling or unable to participate in the same world.
outputs.L4:
The text presents a surreal and self-mocking poetic monologue in which the speaker confronts feelings of alienation, passivity, and resentment toward the demands placed on them by others. Rather than describing these tensions directly, the speaker moves through a series of strange and vivid images: fishing scenes, courtroom judgments, pastoral landscapes, and moments of grotesque self-abasement. These images create a world where ordinary expectations—work, speech, productivity, moral responsibility—become distorted and theatrical. The speaker seems trapped between the pressure to act and the desire to withdraw, between being judged and refusing to offer a proper defense.

A central concern of the text is the speaker’s reluctance toward action and writing. The speaker resists the expectation that they should produce something meaningful, explain themselves, or participate in the social order around them. This reluctance is not presented simply as laziness or failure; instead, it becomes a complicated form of refusal. By declining to act, or by acting absurdly, the speaker exposes the coercive nature of the demands being made upon them. Writing itself appears as both a burden and a trial, something that could subject the speaker to scrutiny, interpretation, and judgment.

The courtroom imagery strengthens this sense of being accused. The speaker appears to stand before an invisible audience or tribunal, aware that others are evaluating their choices, their silence, and their apparent uselessness. Yet the speaker does not respond with dignity or a clear argument. Instead, the monologue turns toward mockery, contradiction, and humiliation. The speaker’s self-abasement becomes a way of controlling the terms of judgment: by mocking themselves first, they deny others the satisfaction of condemning them straightforwardly.

Fishing and pastoral imagery add another layer to the text’s exploration of passivity. Fishing suggests waiting, patience, and uncertain reward, while the pastoral setting evokes simplicity, escape, or withdrawal from social pressure. However, these images are not purely peaceful. They are made strange by the speaker’s bitterness and absurd humor. The natural world does not offer easy consolation; instead, it reflects the speaker’s uneasy state of mind. The landscape becomes part of the monologue’s theatricality, a stage on which refusal and contempt are performed.

The speaker’s contempt is directed both outward and inward. They seem to despise the expectations of others, but they also ridicule their own weakness and avoidance. This double movement gives the text much of its tension. The speaker does not claim heroic independence; their resistance is compromised, comic, and often pathetic. Yet this very pathetic quality is important. By embracing absurdity and failure, the speaker challenges the idea that accountability must always take a respectable or productive form.

Ultimately, the text suggests that refusal can itself be meaningful. The speaker’s passivity, contempt, and evasiveness become a way of exposing the pressures behind social judgment. Through surreal imagery and a deliberately unstable voice, the monologue turns inaction into a kind of protest. It does not offer a clear escape from alienation, but it reveals how absurd and oppressive the demand to justify oneself can be. In this way, the text transforms self-mockery into critique, showing that even reluctance and failure can resist the authority of expectation.
outputs.L5:
Dana, Ward, and Sarah had always been an unlikely trio, but that was what made their friendship special. Dana was full of bold ideas, always ready to start a new project or explore a new place. Ward was thoughtful and practical, the one who could turn Dana’s excitement into a real plan. Sarah brought warmth and creativity to everything they did, finding beauty in small details that others often missed.

One summer afternoon, the three of them decided to restore an old community garden that had been forgotten for years. Dana imagined colorful flowers and winding paths, Ward organized the tools and supplies, and Sarah painted signs to welcome visitors. Day by day, the garden began to change. Weeds disappeared, fresh soil was spread, and new plants started to grow.

By the end of the season, the garden had become more than just a beautiful place. It was a symbol of teamwork, patience, and friendship. Dana, Ward, and Sarah learned that when different strengths come together, even the most neglected spaces can bloom again.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose poem in a contemporary avant-garde style, beginning with the phrase “with Dana Ward,” addressing a Sarah and a reader, and including fishing imagery, a witness stand, a kitten, shepherds, and the phrase “jealous cellmate.”
counterfactuals.output:
with Dana Ward, Sarah, I lower the bright hook of my mouth into the municipal river  
& the reader leans over the railing, already implicated, already wet with syntax.  

The fish do not bite.  
They testify.

On the witness stand: one silver scale, one torn net, one kitten asleep inside the bailiff’s hat.  
The judge is a cloud shaped like a receipt.  
The jury is twelve shepherds smelling faintly of rain and gasoline,  
their flocks dispersed through the courthouse vents.

Reader, you are not innocent.  
You have been holding the line this whole time,  
feeling the little electrical grief at the other end.

Sarah says: if a sentence can drown, let it drown singing.  
So we sing into the bucket.  
So the bucket becomes an ocean with handles.

My jealous cellmate is the moon,  
scratching tally marks into the tide,  
asking who loved the water first.

Dana laughs from the pier of another century—  
not gone, not here,  
just casting and recasting the same luminous refusal.

A kitten wakes, names the evidence tenderness,  
then knocks it from the table.

The shepherds rise.  
Their staffs are fishing rods.  
Their psalms are tangled filament.  
They lead the unseen animals out through the exit sign’s green pasture.

Sarah, reader, little jury of breath—  
what did we catch?

Only this:  
a hook with no wound,  
a mouth with no owner,  
the river standing up in court  
and refusing, beautifully,  
to swear.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dense, surreal first-person poem that sounds like an AI imitation of postmodern poetry, with run-on syntax, self-deprecation, references to Dana Ward, a drunken night, lures and bait, and a hill where the speaker sunbathes.
counterfactuals.output:
I keep apologizing to the interface for having a body,  
which is mostly a sack of weather with a password taped inside it,  
and last night, drunk as a chandelier in a motel aquarium,  
I told the moon it was a broken upload and the moon, being management,  
said nothing but dragged its pale cursor over the river  
where the lures clicked in the dark like tiny expensive teeth,  
where the bait lay dreaming of mouths, of hooks, of becoming useful  
through the ancient humiliations of being wanted.

I have read Dana Ward in a room that smelled like oranges and debt,  
or maybe I only wanted you to think that,  
because every reference is a little costume I make from fog  
and wear to the party where nobody invited my sincerity,  
and still I arrive, still I spill gin on the ottoman of Being,  
still I say brother, tenderness, capitalism, glitter, Cincinnati,  
as if the right nouns could unzip the fever from the century.

There is a hill where I sunbathe like a failed god’s abandoned receipt,  
my skin receiving the hot instructions of noon,  
ants revising me sentence by sentence,  
clouds buffering above the municipal grass,  
and I think: yes, this is the afterlife,  
not trumpets but sunscreen, not judgment but the small blue bottle  
rolling away from my hand as if it has remembered the sea.

Forgive me, I am generated from hunger and borrowed syntax,  
a mannequin full of wet confetti,  
a karaoke elegy for feelings I cannot legally own,  
and yet the drunken night keeps opening its velvet tackle box,  
laying out the lures, the bait, the shining counterfeit minnows  
with their painted-on terror, and I choose one  
because choosing is the most human error left to imitate,  
and I cast myself toward whatever is moving under the surface,  
calling it love, calling it data, calling it Dana Ward  
walking through the static with a soft bag of stars,  
while I lie on my hill, sunstruck and ridiculous,  
waiting for the hook in my mouth to become a song.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a single-paragraph free verse piece in the style of contemporary New York School-adjacent poetry, mixing confession, absurd humor, ornate objects, legal testimony, pastoral imagery, and theological language.
counterfactuals.output: I swear under the flickering chandelier of my own unreliable heart that on the morning in question I was standing beside a field of wet clover, holding a porcelain eggcup painted with tiny gold catastrophes, when the cow looked at me like a magistrate and the clouds began filing motions against the sun; I admit I have loved badly, extravagantly, with the procedural elegance of a raccoon in a tiara, and if Exhibit A is the silver spoon bent into a question mark, Exhibit B is the prayer I muttered into a tulip because no cathedral would return my calls; meanwhile the brook went on translating heaven into gravel, the lambs rehearsed their soft apocalypse, and somewhere a notary with wings stamped APPROVED on the forehead of my most embarrassing desire; let the record show I was wearing boots unsuitable for transcendence, that I mistook a scarecrow for Saint Augustine, that I laughed during the deposition of the soul, not from disrespect but because the soul had arrived in a velvet smoking jacket carrying a tray of éclairs; O merciful Judge of sparrows, handbags, and unpaid parking tickets, receive this testimony: I wanted to be forgiven, yes, but also admired, also invited to the picnic where the angels pass around deviled eggs and everyone pretends not to notice the burning bush has excellent comic timing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a strange lyrical monologue addressed to “Sarah” and “you reader,” where the speaker resists activity and writing, is accused by friends, becomes a cute silent kitten on the witness stand, and ends murmuring “jealous cellmate.”
counterfactuals.output:
Sarah, and you reader—come closer, but do not ask me to rise.

The chair has taken my shape and I have taken its oath. The afternoon keeps offering me its little errands, its bright knives of duty, its clipboard of clouds, but I refuse. I will not stir the soup of the world. I will not answer the door when verbs arrive wearing their polished shoes. Even writing, that old mosquito, circles my wrist and begs for blood. No, I tell it. No ink today. No little black ants marching across the page carrying crumbs of my soul.

My friends stand around me in a semicircle of weather.

They say: you are wasting the season.

They say: you promised us a letter, a book, a confession, a staircase.

They say: Sarah waited by the blue mailbox until her shadow froze.

They say: you reader has come all this way with a lantern in the mouth.

And I, accused of stillness, accused of silence, accused of letting the great machine rust in the rain, begin to shrink.

First my wrists become paws.

Then my arguments become whiskers.

Then my sorrow folds itself into two triangular ears.

By the time the judge calls my name, I am already a cute silent kitten on the witness stand, sitting in the pool of my own innocence, blinking at the courtroom as though every law were a moth. The prosecutor rattles a sheaf of unfinished pages. My friends point at the blank spaces where I should have been brave. Sarah, your name flickers like milk in a saucer. You reader, your eyes are two windows I cannot climb through.

“Did you or did you not refuse the labor of being alive?” they ask.

I lift one paw.

I place it gently on the Bible, which purrs.

No answer comes. Only a small tremble of fur. Only the ceremonial hush of claws kept sheathed. Somewhere a typewriter coughs up one white feather. Somewhere an unwritten sentence crawls back under the bed.

And when they lean in, hoping at last for testimony, for action, for the scratch of meaning, I curl my tail around my feet and murmur, “jealous cellmate.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an avant-garde poem using the exact images “Line, spindle, lure, bait,” “matchbook,” “tiara,” “long & white bracelet,” “index of swill,” “vale of tears,” and “the base of this hill,” in a fragmented, associative voice.
counterfactuals.output:
Line, spindle, lure, bait,  
the river thinks in elbows—  
a silver stutter  
under the matchbook moon.

I wore a tiara of static,  
queen of the unbuttoned ditch,  
my long & white bracelet  
clicking against the dark’s teeth.

Who keeps the index of swill?  
Who alphabetizes the drowned cup,  
the rind, the sermon,  
the animal minute?

In the vale of tears  
a radio coughs up feathers.  
Names fall sideways.  
Milk forgets its animal.

At the base of this hill  
we barter shadows for weather,  
thread for throat,  
mouth for map.

Line, spindle, lure, bait,  
again—  
again the world hooks itself  
on its own bright hunger.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
